newsitem.title: USA: 117,000-year-old footprints found in South Africa.
newsitem.headline: 117,000-year-old footprints found in South Africa.

text.p: A set of 117,000-year-old footprints found in South Africa is possible evidence of a woman who could be the common ancestor of all modern humans, the fossils' discoverers said on Thursday.

Made during a barefoot stroll in wet sand after a rainstorm, the fossilized footprints are an important clue to a period with a scarce fossil record: 100,000 to 300,000 years ago, a time when modern humans emerged.

"These were made by a person who looked anatomically just like us," said Lee Berger, a paleoanthropologist who announced the discovery at a news conference at the National Geographic Society in Washington.
A fiberglass cast of the footprints was displayed at the news conference.

Berger and David Roberts, a South African geologist who actually found the footprints nearly two years ago, referred to the person who made the footprints as "she," based on the prints' relatively small size, but acknowledged that they could also have been left by a small man or a young child.

If the prints were made by a female, she holds the possibility of being the anthropological "Eve," a hypothetical woman who lived somewhere in Africa between 100,000 and 300,000 years ago and carried a particular type of DNA, genetic material passed on only through females.

This hypothetical "Eve" is thought to be the common ancestor of modern humans, and while Berger said it was highly questionable that these prints were hers, he also said the prints were made at the right time and place to fit "Eve"'s profile.
Roberts, of the South African Council for Geoscience, found the footprints in what is now the rocky shore of the Langebaan Lagoon, about 60 miles (96.56 km) north of Cape Town.
The chances of such footprints surviving to this day are "millions to one", Roberts said.

To last this long, the footprints had to be quickly covered after being made, possibly by blowing sand, then buried for a long time to be preserved in rock, then eroded to the point where hardened sediment from the ancient dunes could be chipped away to reveal them again, Roberts said.
What he first saw was a ridge in the rock along the lagoon that showed where the ancient sand had been pushed aside by the side of the woman's foot; the actual footprint was filled with blown sand.

Roberts was looking for footprints in the area because he had already found fossilized tracks of carnivores and rock fragments that had been worked on by hominids in the sedimentary rocks around the lagoon.

Only three other sets of hominid footprints have been found in Africa, and two of these came from more than a million years ago, too early for modern humans. The third set were dated about 30,000 years ago, an eyeblink in the course of human evolution, Berger said.
The Langebaan footprints were dated by studying the surrounding sediments and noting the fluctuations in sea level in the area over time, Roberts said.

The line of footprints stretches away from the shore into what used to be ancient sand dunes which are now buried under rock, and Berger said scientists plan to uncover those additional footprints by creating a "mine" in the rock.
